title: Cole Wehrle - Play as Procedural Generation: Oath as a Roguelike Strategy Game
speaker: Cole Wehrle
talk_title: Play as Procedural Generation: Oath as a Roguelike Strategy Game
description: Can you make a roguelike game without a dungeon? Can you make one without a hero? Is a computer even necessary? In this talk, Cole Wehrle talks about the creation of Oath how he adapted roguelike design conventions to the peculiar demands of a political strategy board game

segments.text: COLE: Thank you very much. I am excited to talk about it because it is a weird game. All right. I
am going to talk about a game I worked on called Oath. It is a little bit of an odd fit or seems
like it is an odd fit for this conference. It is a grand strategy game where players spend time
marching around a map, it is usually about political power struggles trying to hold on
to the thrown or knock another player off that thrown, but despite its grand focus,
it actually has a kind of roguelike origin. A lot of the games that influenced its build were not
paradox or civilization games but roguelikes, CRPGs. I put ultima for NXS. We were playing a
lot of early Cud, and Spelunky and thinking about how that could be adapted to a strategic space.
I don't have time to offer the full design history of the entire game but instead I want to think
about the ways that the game adapted some of the discourse and tools of roguelike design for the
strategy space. If you work in computer games, you have this lovely things called a processor and you
can build super complicated Markov chains. We have players and I do my best to trick them to do all
the computation and that can be hard. Players get distracted or maybe don't play as well as we need
to but they are often playing to win the game and that's a pretty important part of the game.
Victory is a strategic game but it is pretty far from a game's central part in a rogue. In
a game it happens how the player won rather than who happened to win. While oath is a competitive
game it is larger and stranger than that. It is sort of a narrative first but there is no
written narrative. There are no systems for character advancement or named protagonists.
The stories only come into focus when you are not playing the game. It is a game that generates its
meaning in the post-game report. This is all con traditions but it is really a fundamental part
of all games and not just tabletop. Games need places of reflection and encounter in order to
generate meaning. I hope you will indulge me with a little foray into reader response theory because
I really never left grad school and it Marcs me in so many ways. We have the classic theory of reader
response where we have the reader and the author function and where they overlap we have something
that's usually called the transaction. This is the place where the text actually exists as a lived
experience. You can adapt this to games pretty easily. We have games on one side, players on the
other, and then the overlap of play is the moment where the game is kind of coming into life. Now,
like any good theoretical concept, this is going to seem completely obvious to anyone. Of course,
games and players have to work together to create something called the game. We can imagine these
being overlapping spheres. Also as the case with a lot of theory, here we should pause and think
about some of the implications. For one thing, there is a lot of the game that players don't see.
This is important because a player's experience of the game isn't the entire game. It is just the
slice they happen to be exposed to. Likewise, a game team, or designer, can't understand the full
range of a player's experience. That means when a player is playing a game things take valences
that they could not have anticipated because the designer is not every player. This reminds
us of the importance of players. I am one of those designers who reads every comment I can find about
a game I work on which is a sure way to start your day with a small panic attack but I think it
is really important. Every experience of playing a game, even a really negative one, is a kind of
valid experience. It is someone encountering a thing that you invested a lot of your life
and care into and it is producing a response in a player and even if you are not over their shoulder
watching them play a digital game or sitting at the table playing a board game because your
work is there you are in that conversation. We are always participants in the act of play if
we are making games and that can sometimes be a little harrowing. I want to talk about
procedural generation and how Oath uses it. Let's add procedural generation to this formula. When we
put procedural generation in a game it expands the area of play and creates new zones. When building
procedural generation one thing it creates on the side of the game are the unseen possibilities.
Things that a game could have generated but that it didn't. These are parts of the game. They can
happen but they were never experienced. And on the other side, we have a kind of inversion of
that which is the imagined impossibilities. These are the things a player can think might happen in
a game but can never actually be produced in a game. If you were a kid who grew up playing
a lot of roguelikes or I think about my kids playing Minecraft they are always inventing
biomes they heard about on the playground which are these imagined possibilities which are kind
of part of the game even if explicitly not part. And at the bottom we have unused model elements,
parts of the dataset that were not generated, weird relics of the design that got turned off
sometime in testing. When I am digging into the logic or the procedural generation systems there
are whole blocks that aren't used and I want to include them. Tabletop games have a long history
with procedural generation. Usual they are simple. Something as simple as an event table. This is
from a game called mythemic bash land and his game is filled with things called spark tables where he
says if you ever in a panic need something, roll a couple it D12s and we will give you something.
This is used to generate ailments for MPCs so if you encounter someone has nausea or experienced
unexplained blindness, you just throw a couple D12s and you built something. I love a random
table because it allows you to see the full space of a procedural generation in a single screen. It
is so clean and all the part is transparent. For a player, it can be frustrating. About the
third time they ran to a love sick turtle or irritable hermit they are going to realize the
adjectives you are using to prop up the story has a location where they are build. The more a player
understands how the procedural generation works it can undo itself. Some of the games coming out in
the years since, and I am talking about tales of the Arabian nights. Players draw a card on their
turn, maybe you encounter the crystal palace and that will inform which counter matrix you can use.
Maybe it is L and you can attack it or Rob the crystal palace and that will leave the player
to look up in the binder. It is just a choose your adventure model but the layers of obscuring create
this. It is like being on a train in a switch yard but there is a lot of fog so you can't see where
all the tracks are going and it starts to feel like you are in this incredible open world. Now,
there is a limit to this. If you just keep pumping fog into it, it is going to start to
feel like white noise. It is going to start to feel like you lost in an infinite world. I am
reminded of the early procedurally generated first person games like dagger fall where the world felt
empty and foggy. So the key is to remember we aren't just trying to generate content but
content with intention. We are trying to give players the feeling of being in a lived world.
In table top games this could be difficult. As a tabletop designer I often make bespoke content.
Instead of tossing out 10 randomly generated magic swords, I will design each one because
I know the player probably won't see all the items so I can afford to spend time to make
it a little more bespoke. However, when we are playing we have this wonderful resource,
this wonderful generator of bespoke intentional gameplay content, and of course those are our
players themselves. Players are great at inventing stories and providing explanations for how and why
the world behaves that way. And they do this all over the place. They will be scribbling notes on
character sheets in a role-playing game, come up with fan variance, but a lot of this stuff
gets blown away. All of the lovely creativity of a player, a lot of it is circumscribed to the game.
I start to reframe the question a little bit. Is there a way we can capture the ephemeral play? If
the this intentional world play is happening is it possible to pipe it back into the game players are
playing? I know that's certainly possible in the context of a role-playing game but can we make it
work in a board game? With that, I want to talk a little bit about Oath. I think we have all earned
it. Appreciate you allowing me to take some time to talk about theory. The premise of Oath is very
simple. Specifically every in-game state in Oath is also a start state. And this allows
the game to like layer over itself where players each game are painting a picture and then they
are putting like a light top coat and painting another picture on top of it and keep doing this
over and over. The game can always be reset to its factory default state. Nothing is every destroyed.
But it is easier to continue the story. It is OK it players drop, new players come in,
the game just continues going. This allows the game to develop this really amazing backstory
without any pre-written plots. There aren't even proper nouns in this game. It feels organic and
it is organic. It is generated by the players. Now this whole thing only works because the game uses
those little machines of intention, those players, to generate the world that the games are playing
in. To kind of actively build the world as they are playing. Now, this is not a role-playing game.
Players are not given free rein. They can't make Oath into anything they want it to be. Oath is a
game with rules, a rulebook that is so serious we call it the law of Oath because we want to scare
players. It looks like this. It is filled with things players can and cannot do. I could talk
about all the rules on this page and bore you to tears about how each one is contributing to
the overall project of the game but instead I just want to talk about the game's two central
design strategies. The first one is Oath has a selective memory. This is really important.
It remembers how it is played but in a very uneven way. Some things are totally remembered,
some things are going to be partially remembered and have unintended consequences, and there are
some things that are going to be forgotten. Decisions that players make that are not going
to be recorded in any meaningful way. That's the first design strategy. The second design strategy
is the game has a simple decision framework. It boils down very complex decisions in order to
really just to sharpen the feeling of regret when players choose any decision no matter what they
choose which is to say if we sum that up the game has a faulty memory and fills players with regret.
These are the essential characteristics of good history telling and good world building I think.
Let's talk a little bit about that selective memory rushlight. The first and most important
thing is it remembers the territory of its winner. If you think about any strategy game you played,
Risk, the kingdom, empire, state you build at the end of the game is the starting state for the
next world. This is the absolutely core element of the game. All of the parts of the world that

sites we were eradicating a sea and destroying this beautiful geography that was built. One of

sites. You can see a site here. There are only a few important element do is each site. Sites

at Oath. Oath features a deck of six cards Oath features a deck of six suits. There are a lot more

You could go to the forest and muster with the wolves and collaborate with them. You could go to

if you have control of the hospital they will be responding using the hospital's power. These
cards will sit on sites though players have some cards in their personal area most of the cards

game. There are so many cards it is actually a design problem. If you have too much content it
can work against the feeling of intention and the game starts to feel arbitrary like we are playing

for the cards in play. To illustrate what I am talking about, I want to show you this adorable
baby. This is a card from the expansion so not the set out yet called the favorite son. This card is
quite misaligned. People hate this card. They hate it because it is really powerful. One of the ways
you can win is by managing control of the people's love it is called people's flavor. Players compete
for it. If you play the favorite son it short circuits the political race and you instantly win

so mad but then they know in the second game it is still in the deck and that's because though
Oath has this giant roster of cards. The actual play deck is only about 60 cards tall and it is

to compete in the political arena but I know there is a baby going to be born and where is that
baby? It allows players to form deep multi-game relationships with this card and that's because
the deck is holding some game memory. Now nothing in Oath is static and there deck does change. It
changes at a rate of about 10%. Six cards leave the deck every game, six cards enter. When we
were thinking about how we wanted the world of Oath to feel I really focused on a gradual
sensibility. Oath is a generational game. I didn't want players starting in the stone age and end in
a spaceship so we were not doing civilization. We looked at a lot of fashion magazines and thought
about conceptualizing the world as the space of 300 years in the middle ages. Yes, there was a
difference if you were living in Asia minor in 1750 it was different from 1850 and 1950 but the
structures and culture of life were being held from game to game. The second design strategy is
the players of change. What sort of decisions do players make in this world? Oath is a very big
sandbox strategy game but I really tried hard to make the decisions either or. Very simple almost
binary decisions. Here I was inspired by the character creation used in Ultima where players
are being forced to choose one thing over another and to know that the path that they do not take
could potentially haunt them. To illustrate this, I want to show you a mechanical example
from Oath. At the end of the game, the player with the people's favor gets to decide which
cards are going to leave the deck. This has been adjusted for the expansion. The way it works is
they make three piles of three cards and pick two and pick one card that will be their best friend
and the other two cards in the stack are saved and kept. Let's say you barely won the game. The
mercenaries helped you do it and you select them. The wolves and the hospital will be in the deck
but the other six cards including that adorable baby are out of here and added to a pile called

legacies players can earn that are alternate ways of unlocking card powers. Critically at the start

game they will have a hard time juggling several legacies and their own personal
ambitions around trying to win or not win. They will have to choose I really wanted to
earn the chronicle of power but it is my choice of do I get the chronicle power or attempt to win the
game? I want those sharp decisions and the feeling of regret. It is really important in making
players feel like they are building a history that has some consequences. Let's back up a little bit
and talk just for a moment about what the strategy does. If we go back to our little rings here,
what's happened is the procedural generation that sits at the bottom of this conception is just
being replaced by past players. So it could even be the same group of players, however,
because the play group is different from game to game, because players forget, they don't have a

just a few kind of really important elements of the way history works in Oath. I have talked about
what the game is remembering, the decisions the players are making, and the stories being told
but I haven't talked about history writing and that is because it doesn't happen inside of Oath.
Oath does not offer any position for any advantage point where players can look at the past. There is
